title: Intelligent tutoring systems for word problem solving in COVID-19 days: could they have been (part of) the solution?
extended_summary:
This paper addresses two related questions about technology in mathematics education during COVID-19 remote schooling. First, it asks whether mainstream mathematics education research had already produced enough evidence on autonomous, teacher-independent technology use to be useful in emergency remote teaching. Second, it examines whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) could serve as a practical, cost-effective alternative to human one-to-one support for arithmetic and word-problem solving.

The authors begin with a systematic review of empirical studies published in mathematics education journals indexed in Web of Science. The review classifies studies by whether technology use was teacher-mediated or standalone. The review found that almost all studies involved teacher mediation; only a very small number supported autonomous student use, and only one reviewed study used an ITS. Most studies focused on teachers, higher education, or non-compulsory settings, suggesting that research relevant to independent home learning was scarce.

The paper then presents an empirical example using HINTS, a step-based intelligent tutoring system for arithmetic word problems. The intervention involved 133 fifth- and sixth-grade students from one public primary school in Castilla-La Mancha, Spain, during COVID-19 emergency remote teaching. Students completed four weekly online sessions over four weeks, with 28 word problems in total, and all participants had access to devices and internet. The system provided automated validation and short reports, while on-demand hints were disabled to prevent students from relying only on system guidance. Results showed that low-income students were less likely to attend the online lessons, even when technology access was provided, but among participating students there was no statistically significant income gap in performance on the HINTS tasks. The authors conclude that ITSs may help provide individualized mathematics practice in remote settings, but that participation barriers linked to socioeconomic conditions remain a serious challenge.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed article combining a systematic review with an exploratory observational case study, but it is not a randomized trial and the intervention evidence is limited to one school context. The methods provide useful descriptive evidence, yet causal confidence is limited by design and by the small, context-specific ITS sample.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest positive potential for ITSs in middle/elementary mathematics problem solving, especially for maintaining performance across income groups, but the observed effects are small and not clearly causal. The strongest benefit is in implementation relevance rather than demonstrated large learning gains.

interventions.use_case: step-based tutoring for arithmetic and algebraic word problem solving with automated validation of solution steps and configurable on-demand hints; studied here in remote standalone homework-like use during COVID-19 ERT

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a standalone ITS (HINTS) used for arithmetic word problems showed no significant income gap in performance during remote use: low-income and non-low-income students did not differ significantly in problems addressed (t(87)=1.04, p=0.8502, d=0.30) or correctness ratio (t(87)=0.74, p=0.4609, d=0.21). However, prior math grades before school closure were significantly lower for low-income students than non-low-income students (M=6.11 vs 7.25, t(127)=2.57, p=0.0113, d=0.55), indicating baseline inequity even though ITS performance during the intervention was similar.
finding.measure: Mathematics grades prior to closure; number of problems addressed in HINTS; ratio of problems solved correctly in HINTS
finding.study_size: n=133 overall; HINTS performance comparisons n=89 (15 low-income, 74 non-low-income)
finding.effect_size: d=0.55 (pre-closure math grades); d=0.30 (problems addressed); d=0.21 (correctness ratio)
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.08 (pre-closure math grades); SD=8.73/8.81 (problems addressed); SD=0.23/0.24 (problem score ratio)

finding.finding_summary: Participation/attendance in the remote standalone ITS sessions was significantly lower for low-income students, suggesting an engagement barrier rather than a learning-performance gap. The paper reports significant associations between income level and attendance at the first lesson (χ2(1)=6.06, p=0.0138; odds of non-attendance 2.82 times higher for low-income students) and at any lesson (χ2(1)=3.87, p=0.0492; odds 2.29 times higher).
finding.measure: Attendance at the first virtual lesson and attendance at any virtual lesson
finding.effect_size: odds ratio 2.82 (first lesson non-attendance); odds ratio 2.29 (any lesson non-attendance)

finding.finding_summary: The paper combines a systematic review and an empirical COVID-era case study to argue that standalone technology use in mathematics education is rare and underrepresented, especially in compulsory schooling. The review found 174 eligible studies out of 817 records, but only 10 involved standalone use of technology and none used an ITS in standalone mode; this is used to support the claim that mathematics education research has been overly teacher-mediated and not well aligned with remote-learning needs.
finding.measure: Systematic review counts of studies by instructional mode and technology type
finding.study_size: 817 records screened; 174 included studies; 10 standalone-use studies
